title: How the AIES Helps BEA Measure Industry Output
gist: The FRED Blog explains that Census's AIES feeds BEA's industry accounts and annual September GDP revisions, and shows AIES manufacturing shipments tracking BEA manufacturing gross output closely from 2007 to Q2 2026. Differences arise from definitions, notably inventory changes.

insights.claim: The Census Bureau's Annual Integrated Economic Survey (AIES) is a building block of the BEA industry accounts.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Revisions to industry output and GDP statistics trace back to AIES data.
insights.quote: is one of the building blocks of the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) industry accounts

insights.claim: Each September the BEA revises GDP, GDP by industry and state-level statistics in an annual update that incorporates more complete source data, with the AIES a major tool in that effort.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: September annual revisions are a recurring window where AIES-driven data changes can shift reported growth.

insights.claim: Census uses the AIES to benchmark several of its own surveys, which links Census survey work to BEA's accounts.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Benchmarking propagates AIES levels into downstream indicators.

insights.claim: From Q1 2007 to Q2 2026, annual AIES manufacturing shipments and BEA quarterly manufacturing gross output moved together with similar values.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: The two independent series corroborate each other, supporting data reliability.

insights.claim: Converting BEA gross output from quarterly to annual frequency further shrinks the differences with AIES shipments.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Compare series at matching frequency to avoid overstating discrepancies.
insights.quote: Changing the frequency of the BEA data from quarterly to annual further shrinks those differences.

insights.claim: The series differ because AIES shipments count the value of products shipped, while BEA gross output is mainly industry sales or revenue from production and, for manufacturing, also adds changes in inventories of finished goods and work in process.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Inventory build or drawdown explains gaps between shipments and output.
